endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Seek active and direct feedback from aﬀected communities via structured feedback mechanisms or redteaming to monitor and improve outputs.

endorsements.title: Stakeholder-centric participation in large language models enhanced health systems
endorsements.quote: Red Teaming 49 is a proactive participatory approach that involves stakeholders in ‘adversarial’ testing scenarios (e.g., presenting ambiguous or conflicting patient data to assess whether the system generates unsafe, biased, or inequitable clinical recommendations) to identify vulnerabilities and failure cases.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether adding intended users and affected community members to red-teaming of generative AI finds harms that expert red teams miss. The recommendation currently rests on one federal framework and one commentary.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard it targets. Certainty therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsing sources are a framework and a commentary, and neither reports outcome data on whether community participation changes what red teams detect.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language and names red-teaming as one of several ways to gather direct feedback from affected communities. The framework is voluntary. A health system that adopts the practice would be following federal guidance rather than meeting a binding requirement, and the guidance does not specify how participants should be recruited or compensated.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare red-teaming with and without intended users and affected community members on the same generative AI system. Such studies would report the number, type, and clinical severity of harms each group identifies, along with recruitment cost and the time participants contribute. Separate work is needed to document how often expert-only red teams miss harms that affected users later report.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether the practice surfaces harms specific to these groups, and whether recruitment of these groups into red-teaming is feasible, remains unmeasured.
